questions.question: Why is authenticating an MCP server with a single, broad service account risky, even if the server's code has no bugs?
options: It isn't risky at all — service accounts are always safe
Without per-user authorization, any user's AI assistant calling through that server can access anything the broad service account can, regardless of that specific user's actual permissions
Service accounts are slower than individual user accounts
This only matters for read-only tools, never for write actions
questions.explanation: A shared service account with broad access means the MCP server itself has no way to distinguish what a specific requesting user should be allowed to do, effectively granting every user's AI assistant the service account's full access level.

questions.question: What does 'identity passthrough' mean in an enterprise MCP integration?
options: Deleting user identities after each session
Carrying the actual requesting user's identity/token through the AI assistant and MCP client to the server, so authorization can be checked against that specific user's real permissions
Allowing any user to impersonate any other user
A feature that only applies to local, single-user MCP servers
questions.explanation: Identity passthrough ensures the server can enforce authorization based on the specific requesting user's actual permissions, rather than relying solely on a generic service account's broad access.

questions.question: A company's AI assistant is connected to their HR system via an MCP server using one shared admin-level service account. Which question best identifies the security gap?
options: Should we just trust that users will only ask for appropriate information?
Does the server enforce per-user authorization based on each requesting user's actual permissions, or does every request inherit the service account's broad access regardless of who is asking?
Is this system too slow to be usable?
Should we remove the MCP server and use no integration at all?
questions.explanation: The core issue is the absence of per-user authorization: without it, any user's AI assistant can technically perform any action the broad service account is capable of, regardless of that individual user's actual entitlements.
